title: Ephemeral latency creep: triage notes and quick-fixes
content:
Summary:

This is a working triage + runbook sketch for the transient latency creep we observed in the west-1 dedicated GPU pools during the 2025-02-14 afternoon customer surge. Behavior: gradual 15–40% p99 token latency increase over ~90 minutes, not correlated with obvious CPU or GPU utilization spikes. Impact: multiple Dedicated customers experienced slowed streaming responses (mostly short-chat workloads) and one in-progress canary rollback misfired due to delayed health checks.

Purpose of this doc:
- Capture the timeline and signals we used to isolate the source.
- Surface quick mitigations that oncall can run with low blast radius.
- Propose a minimal runbook for future autotriggered remediation.
- Record follow-ups and hypotheses for postmortem.

High-level hypothesis (short):
- Latency creep appears tied to KV-cache fragmentation + stale prefix cache eviction behavior under a workload pattern with many short-lived sessions and bursty prefix reuse. Combined with our autoscaler hysteresis, batching windows stretched and cold-KV misses spiked, increasing per-token generation time without raising GPU utilization much.

Why this is distinct from a noisy neighbor: 
- No single tenant had sustained high GPU usage; telemetry shows many tenants with short high-frequency bursts rather than a single long-running heavy job.
- Allocation and GPU scheduler metrics do not show driver-level throttles or memleak.

Signals we used (what to check fast):
1) Routing/Serving telemetry: per-tenant request rate, per-request cache hit metric (kv_cache.hit_rate), per-request batching wait time (serving.batch_wait_ms).
2) GPU runtime: per-process GPU memory usage (nvtop / exporter), per-GPU SM utilization, kernel invocation latencies.
3) Autoscaler: pool desired vs current replica delta, scale events in last 2 hours, hysteresis timer state.
4) Traces: sample tail-latency traces showing increased KV lookup time and longer batch assemble time.
5) Logs: look for increased kv-cache eviction churn logs (we emit eviction events at debug).

Timeline (concise):
- 14:03: baseline, normal p99 ~180ms for short chat sequences.
- 14:17: multiple small bursts begin (customer churn post-marketing email). p99 climbs to ~260ms.
- 14:30–15:45: gradual climb to 300–420ms p99. GPU util ~60–70% but no memory pressure. kv_cache.hit_rate falls from 0.86 to 0.65 for short requests. Batch wait medians increase 10–20ms.
- 15:47: oncall (Ava) attempted soft-eviction of suspicious ephemeral pods; autoscaler began a scale-up that stalled due to hysteresis config. Health checks for canary timed out; one canary rollback triggered and failed.
- 16:15: manual mitigation (cache warming + temporary reduce min_batch_size) reduced p99 to ~210ms.

Immediate mitigations we ran (and why):
1) Temporary reduce min_batch_size on affected route(s) to favor latency over throughput (route-level override). Why: batching windows were expanding; smaller batches reduce tail for short requests. Command: update route config in console -> rollout immediate.
2) Force a KV-cache trim + warm: trigger a prioritized prewarm job for popular prefixes (ad-hoc script that reads top N prefixes seen in last 10m). Why: reduce cold misses.
3) Bump autoscaler aggressiveness temporarily: reduce scale-up hysteresis from 5m to 60s for pools in region. Why: allow faster accommodation for bursty multi-tenant load.
4) Isolate suspicious ephemeral pods by setting anti-affinity to prefer eviction of pods with >X eviction_events. This prevented the single canary from being impacted further.

Quick runbook sketch (for future oncall):
(Pre-checks — <5 min)
- Open Grafana dashboard linked_artifacts[0] and check: kv_cache.hit_rate, serving.batch_wait_ms, pool GPU util.
- Confirm no GPU driver errors in node-exporter logs.
- Check recent scale events: kubectl get deploy autoscaler-config -n infra -o yaml and grep for lastScaleTime.

(If p99 up and kv_cache.hit_rate down)
1) Route level: toggle route -> reduce min_batch_size and set max_wait_ms lower (command via console or rest API: PATCH /routes/:id/config).
2) KV quick-fix: run prewarm script with last-10m top prefixes (script location: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-scripts/prewarm_kv.sh). Monitor hit rate for 3–5m.
3) Autoscaler: temporarily reduce scale-up hysteresis and queue an immediate scale action. kubectl patch cm autoscaler-config -n infra --type merge -p '{"data":{"scale_up_hysteresis":"60s"}}' then trigger scale: POST /internal/autoscaler/trigger?pool=west-1-dedicated
4) If step 1–3 do not reduce p99 within 15m, consider rolling restart of serving pods in smallest batch (1 pod every 2 min) pinned to oldest alloc timestamps to avoid broad disruption.

Mitigation safety notes:
- Cache trim/warm must be prioritized by prefixes to avoid cold-start storm that increases downstream load.
- Autoscaler changes revert after 30m automatically via scheduled job to avoid leaving aggressive settings.
- Route config changes should be limited to impacted routes; console provides rollout rollback if error.

Instrumentation gaps observed (follow-ups):
- We need an aggregated metric for "prefix churn": count of unique prefixes per minute per pool. Current logs make this slow to compute.
- Eviction event logs are debug-only for performance reasons; make a compact counter-level metric for production (kv_cache.evictions_per_min).
- Per-tenant short-lived session signal is noisy; we should add a lightweight sampling tracer for prefix reuse to identify churny clients.

Post-incident hypotheses to validate (for postmortem):
- H1: prefix churn caused kv-cache fragmentation and a cascading increase in batch assembly time.
- H2: autoscaler hysteresis prevented pools from quickly adding capacity, which lengthened batching windows and pushed more work into each batch creating a feedback loop.
- H3: a small percentage of clients oscillated between many short sessions (clients using chat with very low token counts) and produced disproportionate prefix diversity.

Action items (owners and rough ETA):
- Add kv_cache.evictions_per_min metric and prefix_churn counter — owner: Priya Rao — ETA: 2w.
- Implement auto-revert for autoscaler manual overrides and add audit log entry — owner: Diego Chen — ETA: 1w.
- Create a small safe-run prewarm job (k8s CronJob template + RBAC) and test under load — owner: Ethan Li — ETA: 2w.
- Expand test harness to simulate high prefix-churn workload and evaluate default batch/min settings — owner: eng-serving-runtime — ETA: 3w.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Can we detect prefix churn cheaply in the routing tier and trigger a per-route 'de-latency' posture automatically?
- How often have small marketing bursts historically triggered similar symptoms? correlate with marketing calendar.
- Confirm whether the canary healthcheck timeouts were the result of our route-level change or unrelated network flakiness.

Lower-priority improvements (wishlist):
- Per-route adaptive batching policy that short-circuits to low-batch mode when kv hit rate < threshold.
- Lightweight on-host cache for hot prefixes to reduce RPCs to distributed KV for the short requests.

Appendix: quick commands and links
- Grafana (primary): https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/abc123/gpu-pool-overview
- Trigger autoscaler: POST https://internal-api.redwood/autoscaler/trigger?pool=west-1-dedicated (internal only)
- Prewarm script: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-scripts/prewarm_kv.sh
- Example rollback for route config via API: curl -X PATCH -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"min_batch_size":1, "max_wait_ms":20}' https://api.redwood.internal/v1/routes/route-xyz/config

If this looks reasonable, I'll convert to a proper runbook page in Confluence and schedule the follow-ups. For now keeping as a Drive working doc for rapid edits during postmortem drafting.

-- Ava
